context_before.text: Fig. 1 plots the potentiodynamic polarization behaviour of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys with various aluminium contents $\begin{array} { r } { (x = 0, } \end{array}$ 0.3 and 0.5) in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ solution. The $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys have a wide passive region $(\Delta E > 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { m V }),$, which indicates a tendency of the alloys to passivate. Table 2 summarizes the electrochemical parameters associated with the general corrosion behaviour of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ solution. The corrosion potentials $(E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } })$ of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys were determined to fall from -194 to -206 mV as the aluminium content increased from 0.3 to 0.5 mol; the corrosion current densities $(i _ { \mathrm { c o r r } })$ of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ are $2. 3 9 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ and 5.08 $\times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathsf { A } / \mathsf { c m } ^ { 2 }$, respectively; the $i _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ value dropped to $6. 8 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } { \mathrm { A } } / { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 }$ when aluminium was eliminated from the alloy, as in $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }.$. Furthermore, the critical current density $(i _ { \mathrm { c r i t } })$ increased with the aluminium content, implying that the barrier to passivation increases with the aluminium content. The passive current density $(i _ { \mathrm p a s s })$ of the $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy is lower than that of the Al-containing alloys. Hence, adding aluminium to the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys reduces the resistance to general corrosion in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution when the alloys are in the passive state.

The as-cast $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ (four-component, aluminium-free) alloy is a face-centered cubic (fcc) solid–solution with an a-FeCr structure, according to the XRD patterns (Fig. 2) [18]. However, as the aluminium content increased, the peak intensities of the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase increased. The as-cast $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r } -$ $\mathsf { F e } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 } }$ (five-component) alloy is composed of mixed fcc/bcc phases whereas a single bcc structure was observed for the alloy containing 0.5 mol aluminium. The ferritic stainless steels (such as type 430 stainless steel) are essentially iron–chromium alloys with structures mostly of the bcc a-iron type. However, the austenitic stainless steels (such as type 304 stainless steel) are ternary iron–chromium–nickel alloys, and their structures are of the fcc c-iron type. Indeed, the austenitic stainless steels normally have greater corrosion resistance than the ferritic stainless steels [19]. This fact may suggest why the $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy (fcc structure) is more resistant to corrosion than are the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ $(x = 0. 3$ and 0.5) alloys (bcc structure).

However, as the aluminium content in the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r } -$ $\mathsf { F e } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 } }$ alloys increases from 0.3 to 0.5 mol, the DE falls from 1176 to 1114 mV. Furthermore, a transpassive region exists for the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution. The transpassive breakdown of stainless steels occurs near the oxygen evolution potential where the chromium-rich passive film is unstable. Above the breakdown potential, water is unstable and is oxidized to oxygen gas $(\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } 1 / 2 0 _ { 2 } + 2 \mathrm { H } ^ { + } + 2 \mathrm { e } ^ { - }, E ^ { 0 } = 1. 2 3 \mathrm { V }) [2 0]$. The transpassive dissolution of Cr from the underlying alloy through the passive film $(2 \mathrm { C r } + 7 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } O \longrightarrow \mathrm { C r } _ { 2 } { \bf O } _ { 7 } ^ { 2 - } + 1 4 \mathrm { H } ^ { + } + 1 2 \mathrm { e } ^ { - }, E ^ { 0 } = 0. 3 0 \mathrm { V })$ is also expected in a sulfuric acid medium [21]. A wealth of information is available on the corrosion behaviour of 304 stainless steel that is exposed to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ solutions [22]. Accordingly, a comparison of the corrosion behaviour of HEAs with that of the conventional ferrous alloys, such as 304 stainless steel, is of interest. Table 2 indicates that the Al-free $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy has a wider passive region than the 304 stainless steel. However, the $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ values of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r } -$ $\mathsf { F e } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 } }$ alloys are more active than that of the 304 stainless steel (-186 mV), and the $i _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ values of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys also exceed that of the 304 stainless steel $(7. 4 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 })$ in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$

Although the formation of an oxide film is effective in protecting the HEA, when localized damage of this passive film occurs, pitting corrosion advances rapidly. Fig. 3 presents the potentiodynamic polarization tests of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys in 1 M NaCl solution. Because pitting initiates at the pitting potential $(E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }), E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ may be used as an index of resistance to pitting corrosion: a nobler value of $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ is associated with an increased resistance to pitting [23]. A sharp increase in the anodic current demonstrates the sustained localized breakdown of the passive film. In the present study, the $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ values of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n }.$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys were about equal, and they were significantly lower than for the Al-free $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy. As the aluminium content in the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys increased from 0 to 0.5 mol, the $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ fell from 19 to -123 mV. Therefore, the addition of aluminium to the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys reduces the resistance to pitting corrosion.

The potentiodynamic polarization curves for the Al-free and Alcontaining alloys obtained in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ with various concentrations of NaCl (0–0.5 M) are plotted in Fig. 4. The potentiodynamic polarization curves of the ${ \sf A l } _ { x } { \mathrm { C r F e } } _ { 1. 5 } { \sf M n N i } _ { 0. 5 } \left(x = 0 \right.$ and 0.3) alloys each show a passive region where $\left. \frac { \hat { \sigma } \phi } { \hat { \sigma } \log i } \right| _ { i _ { \mathrm { p a s s } } }$ fi 1 in a Cl<sup>-</sup>-free solution. In all cases, the effect of adding NaCl to the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution is to shift $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ to more active values. Table 3 indicates that the $i _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }$ and $i _ { \mathrm { p a s s } }$ values increase, while DE changes only slightly as the chloride content increases from 0 to 0.1 M. However, at the critical chloride concentration of $0. 2 5 \mathrm { M }, i _ { \mathrm p a s s }$ increases to values that are two orders of magnitude higher than that observed in the Cl<sup>-</sup>-free solution. The existing passive film breaks down when the applied potential reaches the pitting potential, resulting in the nucleation and formation of pits at discrete locations on the metal surface [24]. The presence of chloride in an acid solution generally increases potentiodynamic anodic currents at all potentials; however, the most notable feature here is the sharp increase in current at $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }.$. The current at the $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ increases markedly as the amount of chloride in the sulfuric acid increases, regardless of whether or not aluminium is present. Moreover, as the concentration of chloride increases from 0.1 to 0.25 M, DE falls from 1150 to 495 mV for Al-free $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy, and from 1127 mV to almost no passive region for the Al-carrying $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy. Adding aluminium apparently reduces the ability to develop a passive film on the alloy surface.

Fig. 5 plots the cyclic polarization curves of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys for $(\mathsf { a }) \ x = 0$ and (b) $x = 0. 3 \mathrm { ~ }$, in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution containing 0.25 M of chloride. The black and gray arrows next to the forward and reverse anodic branches indicate the potential scan directions. Negative hysteresis is said to occur when the current density of the reverse scan is less than that of the forward scan whereas positive hysteresis is said to occur when the reverse scan exceeds the forward scan [25]. The negative hysteresis in the reverse scan of the cyclic polarization curve (Fig. 5a) indicates that the $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy is not susceptible to localized corrosion, and that the passive film repairs itself. The positive hysteresis of the cyclic polarization curve (Fig. 5b) demonstrates that pitting of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy can be induced in a Cl<sup>-</sup>-containing solution. The area contained within a positive hysteresis loop is related to the amount of pit propagation that occurs during the cycle, according to Wilde [26]. The small

Electrochemical impedance is a powerful tool in studying corrosion and passivation processes. EIS provides more information than the other electrochemical techniques about the electrochemical processes that occur at the surface. $\mathrm { F i g. }$ 6 shows the effect of aluminium on the Nyquist plot of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ (x = 0, 0.3 and $0. 5)$ alloys in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }.$ The Nyquist plot for the Al-free $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy includes one capacitive loop from high to medium frequencies and one inductive loop at low frequencies. The capacitive loop is related to the double layer capacity, and the presence of the inductive loop reveals that the alloy surface is partly or totally active [27,28]. Moreover, for the higher aluminium-containing $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys, a different behaviour was observed, in that the electrochemical impedance diagrams included two capacitive loops, which are typically related to the presence of an adsorption layer and charge transfer across the metal-electrolyte interface [29].

Moreover, for the higher aluminium-containing $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys, a different behaviour was observed, in that the electrochemical impedance diagrams included two capacitive loops, which are typically related to the presence of an adsorption layer and charge transfer across the metal-electrolyte interface [29].

The CPE exponents $\alpha _ { \mathbf { a d } }$ obtained by fitting the EIS data are 0.72 and 0.78 for the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r } -$ $\mathsf { F e } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 } },$ respectively. The values are consistent with a porous adsorptive film. The $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy has lower $Y _ { 0 - \mathrm { a d } }$ values than that of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy, revealing that the thickness of the adsorptive layer increases with the amount of aluminium in the alloy. $R _ { \mathrm { t } }$ is 24.0 Xcm<sup>2</sup> for the Al-free $\mathrm { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy, and declines to 18.7 and $2 1. 0 \Omega \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for the alloys containing 0.3 and 0.5 mol of aluminium, respectively. The $R _ { \mathrm { t } }$ of the 304 stainless steel $(2 0 5. 0 \Omega \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 })$ exceeds that of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys. Fig. 9 presents the SEM microstructure of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { x } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys after they had been anodically polarized beyond the breakdown potential (>1.25 V) in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }.$ Fig. 9a depicts almost no pitting, except for some general material dissolution on the surface of the CrFe $1. 5 \mathrm { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy. However, a small amount of shallow attack $(\sim 2 5$ lm in diameter and $5 \mathord { - } 1 0$ lm in depth) occurred at the surface of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy (Fig. 9b). Additionally, Fig. 9c shows an example of the localized corrosion (45 lm in diameter and $\sim 5 0$ lm in depth) of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy, which is larger and deeper than that of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy. Fig. 9d displays this localized corrosion of $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloy at higher magnification, and shows a large number of holes on the surface. Aluminium tends to form a porous oxide film in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ and is involved in the galvanic attack of the weaker and more porous oxide region; when the Al content of Fe–Al alloys is less than 20 at%, the passivation behaviour of alloys deteriorates significantly [36]. Electron configuration theory may explain the minimum Al content that is required to fill the Fe atomic level d and thereby modify the surface characteristics [37]. However, the Al contents of the $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 3 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { A l } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { M n N i } _ { 0. 5 }$ alloys are 6.98 and 11.11 at%, respectively, which are significantly lower than 20 at%. Accordingly, the passive films on the surfaces of these alloys are unstable, with breakdown throughout the period of the polarization test.
